reviewer.summary: The report addresses all nine planned claims, and its headline estimates, intervals, and counts match the revised Stage 2 evidence. It also distinguishes citation patterns from causal effects. Before release, make the eligibility-sensitive review result explicit in the main text and correct or substantiate the sampling and ranking descriptions.

issues.problem: “For reviews the estimate was unclear, and the comparison did not establish that the trends differed.” The review slope is inconclusive under both eligibility rules, but the review–article contrast is inconclusive only under the primary rule. The broader-rule interval in T81 excludes zero. The appendix gives both results, but the main text does not explain the difference.
issues.fix: Replace with: “The review slope was inconclusive under both eligibility rules. The review-minus-article slope contrast was 3.21 rank points per doubling (95% interval −0.08 to 6.52) in the primary analysis and 3.34 points (0.07 to 6.64) when works with only their references cited were included. Evidence for a difference therefore depends on the eligibility rule.” Keep C7 as partly reproduced.

issues.problem: “We counted all author entries, even if the person was not identified. The source excluded teams above 100 authors.” The cited tables show a recorded author count and an observed range of 1–100, but do not establish how unidentified authorship entries were handled or whether an upstream exclusion rule produced the cap.
issues.fix: Unless source-construction documentation can substantiate both details, replace these sentences with: “We used the recorded author count as team size. The supplied Columbia-linked extract contained works with 1 to 100 authors.”

issues.problem: “We ranked each score against other sampled works from the same year that qualified for the analysis.” The word “other” implies the focal work was left out, but the weighted midrank in J15 includes that work in both the tied mass and the denominator.
issues.fix: Replace with: “We ranked each score among all sampled works from the same year that qualified for the analysis, including the focal work itself.”

issues.problem: “That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” In the summary, “each work” can be read as every larger-team work. This interpretation applies only to works with negative scores.
issues.fix: Replace with: “For a work with a negative score, more later publications cited it alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.”

issues.problem: “To qualify, a field, subfield or journal needed at least 30 works with one to ten authors, at least four distinct sizes, and at least five works in each of two ranges: one or two authors, and five to ten.” T69 and T70 document which groups qualified and their counts, but their supplied summaries do not verify the exact thresholds, especially the four-distinct-sizes requirement.
issues.fix: Cite the executable group-eligibility rule alongside this sentence, or remove the exact thresholds and report the supported-group counts.

issues.problem: “We sorted OpenAlex record numbers and drew randomly without replacement within groups, using PCG64 with seed 42.” J5 orders by the text work ID, not by its numeric suffix. That distinction matters when recreating the seeded draw.
issues.fix: Replace with: “We sorted the records by their OpenAlex work IDs as text, then drew randomly without replacement within groups using PCG64 with seed 42.”

reader.summary: The main findings are easy to follow, and the worked examples make the disruption score and rank accessible. Two comparisons need clarification: what the unadjusted author estimate drops, and what the intervals for fields and subfields measure. Most other fixes make the result or comparison explicit sooner.

issues.problem: “For each author, we compared disruption ranks for their works on larger and smaller teams, adjusting for publication year and main OpenAlex topic without matching on either. Among 4,107 works, each doubling was associated with a rank 1.85 points lower, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. Without those adjustments on the same works, the decline was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.” It is unclear whether the second estimate still compares works by the same author or drops that restriction along with the adjustments for year and topic.
issues.fix: We compared larger and smaller teams within each author’s work, taking publication year and main OpenAlex topic into account without requiring them to match. Among 4,107 works, disruption rank was 1.85 points lower per doubling of team size, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points lower. Comparing the same works without accounting for author, year or topic gave a decline of 1.73 points per doubling, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points lower.

issues.problem: “The estimated trend was downward in 14 of 20 fields, or 70%, with a 95% interval of 55% to 80%. All 20 fields contained 6,074 works. For subfields, 24 of 34 had downward estimates, or 71%, with an interval of 53% to 76%. All qualifying subfields contained 3,601 works.” The intervals can be read as estimates of how many fields truly have a decline, rather than ranges for how often the fitted trends point downward when the works are resampled.
issues.fix: The estimate pointed downward in 14 of 20 fields (70%; 6,074 works in all) and 24 of 34 subfields (71%; 3,601 works in all). Across repeated draws of the works, the middle 95% of the shares with downward estimates ranged from 55% to 80% for fields and from 53% to 76% for subfields. A downward estimate does not by itself establish a decline.

issues.problem: “To enter the sampling list, a work needed a recorded reference other than itself. It also needed any one of three citation records in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a citation in a later calendar year through 2026, or a recorded citing work published after it.” The last two alternatives sound like the same evidence. The difference is between a yearly count and a link to a specific citing work.
issues.fix: To be eligible for sampling, a work had to list at least one reference other than itself. Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show at least one sign that the work had been cited: a total above zero, a count above zero for a later calendar year through 2026, or a link to a specific citing work published after it.

issues.problem: “Each plotted reference gets the weight of the work listing it, so longer lists contribute more. We also compared each work’s average reference age using sampling weights. Among works themselves cited in the main window, references in ten-author works were 5.20 years newer than in solo works, with a 95% interval of 4.41 to 6.05 years newer among 1,221 works. Without this extra citation filter, the difference was 5.38 years, with an interval of 4.58 to 6.24 years among 1,249 works.” The paragraph switches from weighting individual references to weighting averages for whole works, but the result sounds like it could describe either comparison.
issues.fix: In the plot, each reference gets the weight of the work that lists it, so longer lists count more. For the numerical comparison, we first averaged the reference ages within each work, then weighted those work averages. Among 1,221 works cited in the main window, the average reference was 5.20 years newer for ten-author works than for solo works, with a 95% interval of 4.41 to 6.05 years newer. Without requiring a citation in that window, the gap was 5.38 years, with an interval of 4.58 to 6.24 years among 1,249 works.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main team-size result, though the appendix shows differences for the shorter window and for reviews compared with articles.” The reader has to look in the appendix to find out what changed or whether it affects the conclusions.
issues.fix: Including works with a score of zero because only their references were cited barely changed the main result. The shorter window then showed a slightly steeper estimated decline than the main window, but the difference remained uncertain. The interval for the difference between the article and review trends just excluded zero.

issues.problem: “Reviews and the model of highly cited references gave inconclusive results.” The summary names two analyses without saying what they failed to establish.
issues.fix: We could not tell whether disruption ranks fell with team size for reviews, or whether very highly cited references became rarer at different rates for different team sizes.

issues.problem: “The largest teams drew early attention, as in the original study. It also found later recognition for small teams and disruptive work.” The opening sounds like a claim about how many citations the largest teams received. The result is about when their early citations arrived.
issues.fix: Among works cited in the first two full calendar years after publication, the largest teams received a larger share of those citations in the first year than solo works did. The original study also found earlier attention for larger teams and later recognition for small teams and disruptive work.

issues.problem: “Subtract the count citing it alongside at least one reference.” At this point in the score definition, “one reference” could mean any reference in the later work rather than one from the sampled work’s list.
issues.fix: Subtract the number of later works that cite both the sampled work and at least one of its listed references.

issues.problem: “The fitted share fell faster for ten-author than solo works.” The reader has to look back to recover which share fell and what made it fall.
issues.fix: The model estimated that raising the age cutoff reduced the share of older references faster for ten-author works than for solo works.

issues.problem: “The cutoff sets which publication dates count; it does not reconstruct the index on that date.” The distinction matters, but “reconstruct the index” leaves the reader to work out what date was and was not checked.
issues.fix: We applied the cutoff to the publication dates of citing works, not to the dates when OpenAlex added their records.

reviewer.summary: The report addresses all nine planned claims, and the headline estimates match the revised findings. It appropriately limits the conclusions to this Columbia-linked sample and avoids causal claims. Before release, make the review-versus-article sensitivity explicit, correct the denominator batching description, and document or narrow the unsupported methods details.

issues.problem: “For reviews the estimate was unclear, and the comparison did not establish that the trends differed.” This is true under the primary eligibility rule, but the broader rule changes the interpretation of the contrast. The review slope itself is inconclusive under both rules; the review-minus-article interval crosses zero under the primary rule and narrowly excludes it under the broader rule (T81, F17). The appendix gives the numbers, but the main conclusion does not explain the sensitivity.
issues.fix: Replace with: “The review slope was inconclusive under either rule. The review-minus-article contrast was 3.21 rank points per doubling (95% CI −0.08 to 6.52) when the work itself had to be cited, and 3.34 (0.07 to 6.64) when references-only cases were also eligible. Evidence for a difference therefore depended on the eligibility rule.” Carry that distinction into the comparison table.

issues.problem: “A citing work counted in the first matching batch of references.” The union-count code batches the focal work together with its references. As written, the sentence implies that a later work citing only the focal work would not enter the denominator (J5).
issues.fix: Replace with: “For the denominator, we batched the focal work and its references together. Each later work was assigned to the first batch containing a work it cited, so it was counted only once.” Cite J5.

issues.problem: “To qualify, a field, subfield or journal needed at least 30 works with one to ten authors, at least four distinct sizes, and at least five works in each of two ranges: one or two authors, and five to ten.” The supplied summaries establish which groups qualified, but do not verify the exact 30/4/5 rule.
issues.fix: Cite or include the exact eligibility predicate from the analysis code. If it cannot be supplied, remove the unverified thresholds and report the supported-group counts from T69–T70.

issues.problem: “We counted all author entries, even if the person was not identified. The source excluded teams above 100 authors.” The cited artifacts show a recorded author-count field ranging from 1 to 100, but do not establish how unidentified entries were handled or that the source deliberately excluded larger teams.
issues.fix: Cite the upstream extraction code or documentation for both details. Otherwise replace the sentences with: “We used the recorded author count as team size. In the source frame, recorded counts ranged from 1 to 100.”

issues.problem: “That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” In the opening summary, “each work” could be read as applying to every larger-team work rather than only to works with negative scores.
issues.fix: Replace with: “For a work with a negative score, more later publications cited it alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.”

reader.summary: The main findings are easy to follow, and the worked examples make the score and rank concrete. The key revision is to say that the comparison used as a baseline for the within-author result does not account for author, year or topic. The remaining edits clarify which works, citations or quantities each result describes.

issues.problem: “Without those adjustments on the same works, the decline was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.” In the section on comparing works by the same authors, “those adjustments” sounds like year and topic only. The comparison also drops the adjustment for author. That distinction matters for interpreting the within-author result.
issues.fix: For the same works, a comparison that did not account for author, publication year or topic estimated a decline of 1.73 rank points per doubling of team size, with a 95% interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.

issues.problem: “A larger share of their works scored below zero. That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” The second sentence can sound as if the pattern held for every work by a larger team, rather than for the works that scored below zero.
issues.fix: A larger share of works by larger teams scored below zero. For a work with a negative score, more later publications cited it together with at least one of its references than cited it without any of its references.

issues.problem: “It also needed any one of three citation records in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a citation in a later calendar year through 2026, or a recorded citing work published after it.” The last two conditions sound alike unless the reader can distinguish a yearly count from the record of an individual citing work.
issues.fix: Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show at least one of three signs that the work had been cited: a total citation count above zero, a yearly citation count above zero in a calendar year after publication through 2026, or an individual citing work published after it, even in the same calendar year.

issues.problem: “The largest teams drew early attention, as in the original study.” This sounds like a finding about how many early citations the largest teams received. The result is about when their early citations arrived.
issues.fix: As in the original study, the largest teams received a larger share of their early citations in the first full calendar year than solo authors did.

issues.problem: “We also calculated each work’s share arriving in the publication year, counting citations through the second full calendar year.” The reader has to infer what goes into the denominator and how it differs from the preceding measure.
issues.fix: We also counted citations from publication through the end of the second full calendar year after publication. For each cited work, we calculated what share of that total arrived in its publication year.

issues.problem: “Reviews and the model of highly cited references gave inconclusive results.” The summary does not say what was inconclusive in either comparison.
issues.fix: We could not tell whether disruption rank fell with team size among reviews, or whether highly cited references became rarer at different rates for different team sizes.

issues.problem: “Each plotted reference gets the weight of the work listing it, so longer lists contribute more. We also compared each work’s average reference age using sampling weights.” The switch from weighting individual references to weighting one average per work is easy to miss.
issues.fix: In the figure, each reference gets the sampling weight of the work that lists it. Longer lists therefore contribute more. In a separate comparison, we first averaged the reference ages within each work, then gave each average that work’s sampling weight.

issues.problem: “The middle 95% of the recalculated values gives the confidence interval for one estimate.” This explains how the interval is calculated but not what it tells the reader.
issues.fix: For each result, we used the middle 95% of the estimates from the repeated draws as a confidence interval. It shows how much the estimate might vary with a different sample.

issues.problem: “Figure 4 plots the change per doubling for each field.” The sentence leaves both what changes and what doubles unstated.
issues.fix: Figure 4 shows, for each field, the estimated change in disruption rank for each doubling of team size.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main team-size result, though the appendix shows differences for the shorter window and for reviews compared with articles.” The reader has to go to the appendix to find out what changed.
issues.fix: Including works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited changed the main result little. In the shorter window, the estimated decline was larger. There was also clearer evidence that disruption rank fell faster with team size for articles than for reviews.

reviewer.summary: All nine planned claims are addressed, and the headline estimates match the revised Stage 2 evidence. The report appropriately limits its conclusions to the sampled works and avoids causal claims. Before release, correct the descriptions of the unadjusted author model and the citation-counting procedure, substantiate or narrow the author-count description, and qualify the review–article conclusion by eligibility rule.

issues.problem: “Without those adjustments on the same works, the decline was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.” In context, “those adjustments” reads as year and topic only. T79 shows that the 1.73-point estimate also omits author fixed effects.
issues.fix: Replace with: “On the same 4,107 works, the unadjusted model, with no year, topic or author fixed effects, estimated a decline of 1.73 points per doubling (95% interval: 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline).”

issues.problem: “A citing work counted in the first matching batch of references.” The union-count algorithm batches the focal work together with its references. A later work that cites only the focal work must also enter the denominator (J5, T33).
issues.fix: Replace with: “For the denominator, we batched the focal work and its references together and counted each later work in the first batch containing an item it cited.”

issues.problem: “We counted all author entries, even if the person was not identified. The source excluded teams above 100 authors.” The cited evidence shows that the analysis used a recorded author count and that the supplied frame spans 1–100 authors. It does not establish how unidentified authors were counted or where the upper limit was imposed.
issues.fix: Cite the extraction or author-count documentation that establishes both rules, or replace the sentences with: “We used the recorded author count. The supplied frame contained works with 1 to 100 authors.”

issues.problem: “For reviews the estimate was unclear, and the comparison did not establish that the trends differed.” That is true under the primary eligibility rule, but the broader analysis gives a review-minus-article interval that narrowly excludes zero. The appendix reports this, but the prose conclusion does not distinguish the two results (F17, T81).
issues.fix: Replace with: “The review slope was inconclusive under both eligibility rules. The review–article contrast included zero in the primary analysis, but narrowly excluded it when works cited only through their references were included (+3.34 rank points per doubling, 95% interval 0.07 to 6.64).”

issues.problem: “That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” In the summary, “each work” could be read as every work by a larger team rather than only the works with negative scores.
issues.fix: Replace with: “For a work with a negative score, more later works cited it alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.”

issues.problem: “The original study also compared company patents and Nobel-winning work and tracked team sizes over decades.” This names the C9 context but leaves out the original Nobel finding and the direction of the historical trend.
issues.fix: State that the original study reported rising average team size from 1954 to 2014 and found Nobel-winning papers unusually disruptive. Keep the distinction between the local comparison of recorded acknowledgments and the original comparisons that were not testable here.

reader.summary: The main finding is easy to follow, and the worked examples make the disruption score and rank clear. The main revision is to distinguish the comparison within authors from the comparison that does not account for author. A few smaller edits would make the eligibility rules, timing measures and comparisons easier to read on the first pass.

issues.problem: “For each author, we compared disruption ranks for their works on larger and smaller teams, adjusting for publication year and main OpenAlex topic without matching on either. Among 4,107 works, each doubling was associated with a rank 1.85 points lower, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. Without those adjustments on the same works, the decline was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.” It is unclear whether the second estimate still compares works by the same author, and whether the first is one overall trend or a separate trend for each author.
issues.fix: We estimated one overall trend by comparing larger and smaller teams for the same author. We accounted for publication year and the main topic assigned by OpenAlex, but the works did not have to share a year or topic. Among 4,107 works, disruption rank fell by an estimated 1.85 points per doubling of team size, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. Using the same works without accounting for author, year or topic, the estimated decline was 1.73 points per doubling, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points.

issues.problem: “A larger share of their works scored below zero. That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” The second sentence sounds as if this happened for every work from a larger team, not just for the works that scored below zero.
issues.fix: Works by larger teams more often had a negative disruption score. A score is negative when more later publications cite the work with at least one of its references than cite it without any of them.

issues.problem: “It also needed any one of three citation records in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a citation in a later calendar year through 2026, or a recorded citing work published after it.” The last two conditions sound like the same check.
issues.fix: Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show at least one of three signs that the work had been cited: a total count above zero, a yearly count above zero in a later calendar year through 2026, or a link to a citing work published after it.

issues.problem: “We also calculated each work’s share arriving in the publication year, counting citations through the second full calendar year.” The reader has to infer both what the share counts and when its denominator starts.
issues.fix: For each work, we counted citations from publication through the end of the second full calendar year. We then calculated the share that arrived in the publication year.

issues.problem: “The least-cited group fell by 2.50 rank points per doubling, with a 95% interval of 1.64 to 3.39 points of decline among 3,277 works.” The group did not fall; its estimated disruption rank did.
issues.fix: Among the 3,277 works in the least-cited group, disruption rank fell by an estimated 2.50 points per doubling of team size. The 95% interval was 1.64 to 3.39 points of decline.

issues.problem: “Each plotted reference gets the weight of the work listing it, so longer lists contribute more. We also compared each work’s average reference age using sampling weights.” The change from counting references to counting works is easy to miss, and the main text does not say how reference age was measured.
issues.fix: We measured reference age as the difference in publication years. In the figure, each reference carries the sampling weight of the work that lists it, so longer lists count more. In a separate comparison, we first averaged the reference ages within each work and then applied the weight once per work.

issues.problem: “Reviews and the model of highly cited references gave inconclusive results.” This does not say what was uncertain in either comparison.
issues.fix: For reviews, we could not tell whether disruption rank fell as team size grew. For highly cited references, we could not tell whether citation counts became rarer at different rates for different team sizes.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main team-size result, though the appendix shows differences for the shorter window and for reviews compared with articles.” The two exceptions are named without saying what changed.
issues.fix: Including works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited barely changed the main result. With those works included, the estimated decline was slightly steeper in the shorter window, but the difference between windows was still unclear. Disruption rank fell more steeply for articles than for reviews under this broader rule.

issues.problem: “Per doubling, rank fell by an estimated 3.75 points without a recorded acknowledgment and rose by an estimated 0.52 points with one; only the decline was clear.” At the start of a new comparison, the reader has to recall what doubles, which rank is measured and which team sizes are included.
issues.fix: Among works with one to ten authors, each doubling of team size was linked to an estimated drop of 3.75 disruption rank points without a recorded funding acknowledgment and a rise of 0.52 points with one. Only the drop was clear.

issues.problem: “The source excluded teams above 100 authors.” It is unclear whether OpenAlex excludes these works or the authors excluded them from the list they sampled.
issues.fix: The list we sampled from excluded works with more than 100 authors.

issues.problem: “The cutoff sets which publication dates count; it does not reconstruct the index on that date.” The second clause is abstract and makes the reader work out what the cutoff does not control.
issues.fix: The cutoff applies to when citing works were published, not to when OpenAlex recorded them.

reviewer.summary: All nine planned claims are addressed, and the headline estimates and intervals agree with the cited Stage 2 findings. The report appropriately limits causal and population-wide conclusions. Before release, correct the rank and citation-count methods descriptions, narrow the author-count provenance claims, and make the review sensitivity result explicit in the main text.

issues.problem: The sentence “We ranked the same 4,405 works with one to ten authors and a citation in both windows, separately for each window” confuses the rank reference set with the slope sample. T71, T82, T84 and J15 show that the ranks were computed among all 5,671 paired eligible works, within publication year, before fitting the slope on 4,405 works. The earlier phrase “against other sampled works” also incorrectly suggests that the focal work was excluded from its own weighted midrank.
issues.fix: In the methods, say that each score was ranked among all eligible sampled works from the same year, including the focal work. In C8, say: “For each window, we recalculated within-year ranks among the 5,671 works cited in both windows. We then fitted the two slopes on the same 4,405 works with one to ten authors.”

issues.problem: “For reviews the estimate was unclear, and the comparison did not establish that the trends differed” does not specify the eligibility rule. The review slope was inconclusive under both rules, but the review–article contrast narrowly excluded zero when references-only cases were admitted (F17, T81). The appendix gives both results, but the main claim assessment does not distinguish them.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with: “The review slope was inconclusive under both eligibility rules. The review–article contrast was inconclusive in the main analysis; when references-only cases were admitted, the review slope was 3.34 rank points per doubling higher than the article slope (95% interval 0.07 to 6.64).”

issues.problem: “A citing work counted in the first matching batch of references” misdescribes the union count. J5 shows that the ordered batches included the focal work ID as well as its reference IDs; a work citing only the focal work still entered the union.
issues.fix: Replace with: “For the union count, we batched the focal work ID together with its reference IDs and assigned each citing work to the first batch containing any ID it cited.”

issues.problem: “We counted all author entries, even if the person was not identified. The source excluded teams above 100 authors.” The cited evidence shows that the analysis used the snapshot’s stored author count and that its observed range was 1–100. It does not establish how unidentified entries were counted or whether the source applied an upstream exclusion.
issues.fix: Replace with: “We used the author count stored in the supplied OpenAlex snapshot. In that snapshot, recorded team sizes ranged from 1 to 100.” Retain the stronger provenance statements only if an extraction artifact documents them.

issues.problem: “We also calculated each work’s share arriving in the publication year” could be read as using the same eligibility rule as the preceding first-full-year analysis. The publication-year share includes a different set of works, and the sign groups use main-window scores (T78, J15).
issues.fix: State that the publication-year share was calculated for works with at least one citation from publication through the end of the second full calendar year, and that negative and positive groups were defined using main-window disruption scores.

issues.problem: “Partly testable” describes the availability of a proxy for C9 rather than giving the original-study comparison a reproduction status.
issues.fix: In the funding section and summary table, use “Not testable as an original-study comparison” and retain the recorded-acknowledgment gradient as a descriptive local result.

reader.summary: The main findings and the worked example for the disruption score are easy to follow. Two methods need clarification before the report is ready: which works count when calculating a disruption rank, and what the comparison by author holds constant.

issues.problem: “For each author, we compared disruption ranks for their works on larger and smaller teams, adjusting for publication year and main OpenAlex topic without matching on either. Among 4,107 works, each doubling was associated with a rank 1.85 points lower, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. Without those adjustments on the same works, the decline was 1.73 points, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.” It is unclear whether the second estimate still compares works by the same author. “Without matching on either” does not explain what the first estimate does.
issues.fix: We compared works by the same author on larger and smaller teams, also accounting for differences across publication years and OpenAlex topics. Among 4,107 works, disruption rank fell by an estimated 1.85 points per doubling of team size, with a 95% interval of 0.27 to 3.43 points of decline. Comparing the same works without accounting for author, year or topic gave a decline of 1.73 points per doubling, with an interval of 0.46 to 3.01 points of decline.

issues.problem: “We ranked each score against other sampled works from the same year that qualified for the analysis. On the scale from 0 to 100, add the percentage with lower scores to half the percentage tied, using sampling weights for both. If weights total 100, with 40 below and 20 tied, the rank is 50.” The word “other” suggests leaving out the work being ranked. The example does not say whether that work is included in the tied weight.
issues.fix: To rank a work, use all eligible sampled works from its publication year, including the work itself. Add the weighted percentage with lower scores to half the weighted percentage with the same score. This gives a rank from 0 to 100. If the weights total 100, with 40 for lower scores and 20 for the same score, the rank is 50.

issues.problem: “It also needed any one of three citation records in our copy of OpenAlex: a positive total citation count, a citation in a later calendar year through 2026, or a recorded citing work published after it.” The last two records sound like the same thing. One uses yearly counts; the other uses the date of a specific citing work.
issues.fix: Our copy of OpenAlex also had to show one of three signs that the work had been cited: a total citation count above zero, a yearly count showing a citation in a later calendar year through 2026, or a record of a citing work published after it, even in the same calendar year.

issues.problem: “The curves show observed lists, not models. The age model assumes that raising the age cutoff by one year reduces the share of older references by the same fraction each time. The fitted share fell faster for ten-author than solo works. The citation model assumes that doubling a citation count reduces the predicted share with exactly that count by the same fraction each time. Among references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether that fraction differed by team size. Neither model fit closely.” “The fitted share fell faster” makes the reader look back to see what share fell and what was changing.
issues.fix: The curves show the data, not the model estimates. The age model assumes that with each extra year of age, the share of references older than that age drops by the same fraction. The model estimated a larger drop for ten-author works than for solo works. The citation model assumes that each doubling of the citation count reduces the share of references with exactly that many citations by the same fraction. Among references with at least 50 citations, we could not tell whether that drop differed by team size. Neither model described the data closely.

issues.problem: “A larger share of their works scored below zero. That means more later publications cited each work alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of them.” “Each work” can be read as every work by a larger team, not just those with negative scores.
issues.fix: A larger share of works by larger teams scored below zero. For a work with a negative score, more later publications cited it alongside at least one of its references than cited it without any of those references.

issues.problem: “Each plotted reference gets the weight of the work listing it, so longer lists contribute more. We also compared each work’s average reference age using sampling weights.” The second sentence leaves it unclear whether the weights are applied when averaging references within a work or when averaging across works.
issues.fix: In the figure, each reference gets the sampling weight of the work that lists it, so longer lists contribute more. For the comparison of average ages, we first averaged reference ages within each work, then used sampling weights to average across works in each team-size group.

issues.problem: “We used works from 2021 through 2023. For each work cited in either of the two full calendar years after publication, we calculated the share arriving in the first.” “The share arriving” does not say explicitly which citations are in the denominator.
issues.fix: For works published from 2021 through 2023, we counted citations in the two full calendar years after publication. For each work cited in that period, we calculated the share of those citations that came in the first year.

issues.problem: “For most intervals we repeatedly drew from the original sample within each team-size group, allowing repeats. This is called a bootstrap. The middle 95% of the recalculated values gives the confidence interval for one estimate.” “Allowing repeats” could mean repeating the draw rather than allowing a work to appear more than once in a draw. The passage explains how the interval is calculated but not what it conveys.
issues.fix: To show how much an estimate might vary from sample to sample, we usually drew again from each team-size group and recalculated the estimate many times. A work could appear more than once in a draw. This is called a bootstrap. The middle 95% of the recalculated estimates gives the confidence interval.

issues.problem: “All 20 fields contained 6,074 works.” and “All qualifying subfields contained 3,601 works.” Both sentences can be read as giving a count for each field or subfield rather than a combined total.
issues.fix: The 20 fields contained 6,074 works in total. The qualifying subfields contained 3,601 works in total.

issues.problem: “Reviews and the model of highly cited references gave inconclusive results.” The summary does not say which questions remained unanswered.
issues.fix: We could not tell whether disruption rank fell with team size for reviews, or whether the rate at which highly cited references became rarer differed by team size.

issues.problem: “Including works that scored zero because only their references were cited in the relevant window barely changed the main team-size result, though the appendix shows differences for the shorter window and for reviews compared with articles.” The sentence packs the inclusion rule, the main result and two exceptions into one sentence.
issues.fix: The main team-size result barely changed when we included works whose references were cited but that were not themselves cited in the same window. These works scored zero. Including them changed some estimates for the shorter window and for the comparison of reviews with articles; see the appendix.

issues.problem: “The cutoff sets which publication dates count; it does not reconstruct the index on that date.” “Reconstruct the index” is abstract and leaves the reader to infer which dates were used.
issues.fix: The cutoff applies to when citing works were published, not to when OpenAlex added their records.
